title: 1984, George Orwell
subject: litterature
description: Published in 1949, 1984 invents Big Brother, Newspeak and the Ministry of Truth. Orwell describes a society where state surveillance and lies crush the individual to the point of tyrant love.

hero.hook: A novel so powerful that its words are still used to name state surveillance and lies.

blocks.text: In **1949**, **George Orwell** published **1984**, one of the most read dystopias in the world. It's not just a novel of anticipation: it's a vocabulary to talk about modern oppression. **Big Brother**, the **[[Newspeak (Newspeak)]]**, the **Ministry of Truth**: these words have left fiction to describe political reality.

Orwell wrote this book while he was seriously ill with tuberculosis on the island of Jura in Scotland. His pessimism comes from concrete experience of politics, war and institutionalized lies. **1984** does not predict the future like a calendar. It describes a mechanism of domination that the author observed closely, from Republican Spain to **Oceania**, the fictional state where everything is controlled.

sections.title: The trauma of Spain: the genesis of Orwellian thought

blocks.text: **George Orwell**, whose real name is **Eric Arthur Blair**, does not invent **1984** in a vacuum. In **1936-1937**, he fought in Spain in the **[[POUM]]** militias. Wounded by a bullet in the neck, he witnesses an internal purge: Stalinist agents hunt down their anti-Stalinist allies as if they were enemies. What marks him the most is not only the violence of the fighting, but the falsification of the facts.

blocks.caption: George Orwell, writer and witness to the totalitarian excesses of the 20th century.

blocks.text: Orwell writes **1984** on the island of Jura, Scotland, tuberculous and without heat. He died in January 1950, seven months after publication.

He sees newspapers rewriting the past, erasing fighters through photographic retouching, transforming allies into traitors overnight. This obsession with state lies directly nourishes the novel. Where **Animal Farm** uses a fable to critique politics, **1984** delves into the human soul under pressure. Orwell is also inspired by **[[Soviet totalitarianism as a model]]**, but his novel goes beyond Stalin: it describes a power which claims to control reality itself, to the point of imposing that **2 + 2 = 5**.

sections.title: The control architecture: the Oceania system

blocks.text: In **1984**, the State occupies all the mental space. **Oceania**, led by **Ingsoc**, is based on four paradoxical ministries: Peace makes war, Abundance organizes scarcity, Love tortures, Truth makes lies. **Winston Smith**, hero of the novel, works at the **Ministry of Truth**: his job consists of erasing the past so that it corresponds to the Party's present.

blocks.caption: Propaganda and control: the visual imagination of totalitarian power.

blocks.text: At the center of the system, the **[[Doublethink]]**: accepting two contradictory truths at the same time, without feeling contradiction. **telscreens** broadcast propaganda and monitor every move. The Party's slogan sums it all up: "He who controls the past controls the future." He who controls the present controls the past. » The **[[Newspeak (Newspeak)]]** reduces the vocabulary to make critical thinking impossible: the fewer words we have to name the revolt, the less we can conceive it.
War is peace. Freedom is slavery. Ignorance is strength.

sections.title: Winston and Julia: the fragility of internal dissent

blocks.text: Winston and **Julia** attempt an intimate rebellion: clandestine love, secret diary, memory of the authentic past. But the Party doesn't just stop them. In **Room 101**, he uses Winston's most visceral phobia, rats, to break him psychologically. He betrays Julia with a panicked cry: “Do it to Julia!” Not mine! »

The ending is terrible: Winston not only obeys, he loves **Big Brother**. Totalitarianism wins psychologically, not just politically. The final image of a boot crushing a face sums up a power that no longer seeks the common good, but power itself, without end. Today, we speak of “Orwellian” practices to designate language manipulation, mass surveillance or **[[Censorship]]**. The novel remains a warning: the truth of the facts is the first line of defense against oppression.

blocks.text: **1984** shows how a state can destroy not only freedom, but the very desire for freedom. Orwell reminds us that factual truth is the first line of defense against oppression.
